los.text: Identify the main components of the spinal cord (ascending sensory tracts, descending motor tracts, dorsal and ventral roots, grey and white matter) and link to the functional consequences of damage at different points along the pathway
los.html:
Grey matter(butterfly)Dorsal horn (sensory), ventral horn (motor neurons), lateral horn T1–L2 (sympathetic). White matter: dorsal, lateral and ventral columns of tracts.
RootsDorsal root (sensory; cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion) and ventral root (motor) join to form the spinal nerve in the intervertebral foramen.
TractCarriesCrossesLesion effect
Dorsal columns (gracile, cuneate)Fine touch, vibration, proprioceptionMedullaSame-side loss below the lesion; sensory ataxia (Romberg's positive)
SpinothalamicPain, temperature, crude touchWithin 1–2 segments of entry (anterior white commissure)Opposite-side loss below the lesion
Lateral corticospinalVoluntary movementMedulla (pyramids)Same-side UMN weakness below the lesion
SpinocerebellarUnconscious proprioceptionUncrossed / double-crossedSame-side ataxia
LesionPattern
Brown-Séquard (hemisection)Same side: weakness, lost proprioception/vibration; opposite side: lost pain and temperature
Anterior cord (anterior spinal artery)Weakness and lost pain/temperature; dorsal columns spared
Central cord (syringomyelia, hyperextension in the elderly)Cape-like pain/temperature loss; arms weaker than legs
Dorsal columns (B12 deficiency, tabes)Lost proprioception and vibration, positive Romberg's
Ventral horn (polio, MND)LMN weakness: wasting, fasciculation, reduced reflexes

los.text: Describe the structures forming the vertebral column, its regions and functions
los.html:
RegionVertebraeCurve
Cervical7Lordosis
Thoracic12Kyphosis (primary curve)
Lumbar5Lordosis
Sacrum5 fusedKyphosis (primary curve)
Coccyx3–5 fused
Functions
  • Supports the head and trunk and passes weight to the pelvis
  • Protects the spinal cord and nerve roots
  • Allows movement
  • Attachment for muscles and ribs
  • Haemopoiesis.
CurvesPrimary (thoracic, sacral) present at birth; secondary (cervical, lumbar) develop with head holding and walking.

los.text: Label a diagram of a vertebra, and differentiate between atlas and axis, cervical, thoracic and lumbar vertebrae and sacrum
los.html:
• Typical vertebra: body (weight bearing) + vertebral arch (2 pedicles, 2 laminae) enclosing the vertebral foramen
    • spinous process, 2 transverse processes, 4 articular processes (facets).
TypeDistinguishing features
Atlas (C1)No body, no spinous process; anterior and posterior arches, lateral masses with kidney-shaped facets for the occipital condyles
Axis (C2)Dens (odontoid peg) projecting up from the body; large bifid spinous process
Cervical
  • Foramen transversarium (vertebral artery, C6 upwards)
  • Small body
  • Bifid spinous process
  • Triangular vertebral foramen
  • Uncovertebral joints.
  • C7 has a long, non-bifid spine (vertebra prominens)
ThoracicCostal facets on the body and transverse processes for ribs; heart-shaped body; long spinous process pointing down; round vertebral foramen
LumbarLarge kidney-shaped body; short square spinous process; triangular foramen; mamillary processes; facets face medially/laterally (limits rotation)
Sacrum
  • 5 fused vertebrae
  • Sacral promontory, sacral foramina (anterior and posterior), alae, sacral hiatus (caudal block), auricular surface for the SI joint

los.text: Explain the main anatomical features of vertebral bones on the bones themselves, on suitable radiographs and other images
los.html:
Lateral X-ray
  • Check the alignment of three lines (anterior vertebral, posterior vertebral, spinolaminar), the bodies, disc heights, and the dens
  • Must show C7/T1 (swimmer's view or CT if not).
APSpinous processes in line, pedicles visible on both sides ("winking owl" sign: missing pedicle in metastasis).
Open-mouth viewDens and lateral masses of C1 (Jefferson and dens fractures).
Oblique lumbar"Scottie dog"; a collar on its neck = pars interarticularis defect (spondylolysis).
CT for bone injury; MRI for discs, cord, nerve roots and ligaments.

los.text: Recognise the anatomy of intervertebral joints and intervertebral discs, and explain the role of the discs in weight bearing in the vertebral column
los.html:
JointTypeDetail
Intervertebral discSecondary cartilaginous (symphysis)Nucleus pulposus (gel, ~80% water) inside the annulus fibrosus (concentric lamellae of fibrocartilage); no discs between C0/C1 or C1/C2
Facet (zygapophyseal) jointsSynovial planeGuide and limit movement; osteoarthritis causes back pain
Uncovertebral (C3–7)Synovial-likeOsteophytes narrow the intervertebral foramen
Weight bearingThe nucleus spreads compressive load outwards onto the annulus (hoop stress) and evenly onto the endplates, acting as a shock absorber.
AgeingThe nucleus dries out → discs lose height (we lose height through the day and with age), annulus fissures.
Blood supplyDiscs are avascular in adults (nourished by diffusion through endplates), so they heal poorly.

los.text: Describe common disc lesions that may impinge upon spinal nerves and/or the spinal cord
los.html:
• Disc prolapse: nucleus herniates through a weakened posterolateral annulus (the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrow and strongest centrally).
LevelRoot compressedSigns
L4/5L5 (the root passing down to the next foramen)Weak big toe extension and dorsiflexion; numb dorsum of foot and big toe
L5/S1S1Weak plantarflexion, lost ankle jerk, numb lateral foot and sole
L3/4L4Weak knee extension, reduced knee jerk, numb medial leg
C5/6C6Weak elbow flexion, reduced biceps/brachioradialis reflexes, numb thumb
C6/7C7Weak triceps, reduced triceps jerk, numb middle finger
Cervical ruleThe nerve root is numbered after the vertebra below the disc (C6 root exits above C6), so a C5/6 disc hits C6.
Lumbar rule
  • a posterolateral prolapse hits the traversing root (the one numbered after the vertebra below), not the root exiting at that level
  • a far-lateral prolapse hits the exiting root.
  • Central prolapse below L1: cauda equina syndrome (saddle anaesthesia, retention, bilateral leg symptoms) → emergency MRI and decompression.
  • Above L1 or in the neck: cord compression (UMN signs).
Straight leg raiseStretches L5/S1 roots (sciatica); femoral stretch test for L2–4.

los.text: Explain the functions of the atlanto-occipital and atlanto-axial joints in the movements of the head, naming the main muscle groups involved
los.html:
JointTypeMovementMuscles
Atlanto-occipital (C0/C1)Synovial (condyloid)Flexion and extension ("yes"); some lateral flexionFlexors: longus capitis, rectus capitis anterior; extensors: rectus capitis posterior major and minor, obliquus capitis superior, semispinalis capitis, splenius capitis
Atlanto-axial (C1/C2)Median: synovial pivot (dens in a ring of anterior arch + transverse ligament); lateral: synovial planeRotation ("no"): ~50% of all neck rotationObliquus capitis inferior, rectus capitis posterior major, splenius capitis, SCM (opposite side)
Transverse ligament
  • Holds the dens against the anterior arch of C1
  • Rupture or laxity (rheumatoid arthritis, Down syndrome) lets the dens compress the cord.
Alar ligamentsDens to the occipital condyles, limit rotation.

los.text: Identify the range of movement of the entire vertebral column and its individual regions
los.html:
RegionFlexion/extensionLateral flexionRotation
CervicalLargeLargeLarge (half at C1/C2)
ThoracicSmall (ribs, thin discs)ModerateModerate (facets in a coronal plane allow it)
LumbarLarge (especially L4–S1)ModerateVery little (sagittal facets lock it)
Whole columnFlexion ~80°, extension ~25°, lateral flexion ~35° each side, rotation ~45° each side at the lumbar/thoracic level.
Schober's testMeasures lumbar flexion (reduced in ankylosing spondylitis).

los.text: Identify the principal muscle groups and ligaments of the vertebral column and surface features in order to be able to perform an examination of the back
los.html:
GroupMusclesNerve
Superficial (move the upper limb)Trapezius, latissimus dorsi, rhomboids, levator scapulaeXI, thoracodorsal, dorsal scapular
Intermediate (respiratory)Serratus posterior superior and inferiorIntercostal nerves
Deep (intrinsic)Erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis: "I Love Spine"), transversospinalis (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores), spleniusPosterior rami
LigamentPositionRole
Anterior longitudinalFront of bodies, wideLimits extension
Posterior longitudinalBack of bodies (inside the canal), narrowLimits flexion; directs prolapses posterolaterally
Ligamentum flavumBetween laminae, elastic (yellow)Keeps the posture upright; hypertrophy → spinal stenosis; felt as a "give" in LP
Interspinous, supraspinousBetween spinous processesLimit flexion
Ligamentum nuchaeNeck: C7 spine to the skullMuscle attachment
  • Surface features for back examination: C7 (vertebra prominens)
    • T3 (spine of scapula root)
    • T7 (inferior angle of scapula)
    • L4 (iliac crests, Tuffier's line)
    • S2 (posterior superior iliac spines, dimples of Venus)
    • paraspinal muscles
    • scoliosis, kyphosis, lordosis.

los.text: Discuss the functional role in stability and movement of the vertebral column and describe the anatomical basis of back pain
los.html:
StabilityBones and facets (shape), discs, ligaments (passive) plus muscles (active: erector spinae, multifidus, abdominal wall, especially transversus abdominis via intra-abdominal pressure).
MovementSmall movements at each segment add up; facet orientation decides which movements each region allows.
Pain sourceMechanism
Muscles and ligaments (most common, "mechanical")Strain, poor posture, deconditioning
DiscAnnular tears (innervated outer third), prolapse with root irritation (sciatica)
Facet jointsOsteoarthritis; worse on extension
Spinal stenosisLigamentum flavum, facet and disc changes narrow the canal → neurogenic claudication, eased by leaning forward
SpondylolisthesisSlip of one vertebra on another (pars defect)
Red flagsCancer, infection, fracture, cauda equina, inflammatory (ankylosing spondylitis)
  • Innervation: sinuvertebral (recurrent meningeal) nerves supply the outer annulus, posterior longitudinal ligament and dura; posterior rami supply facets and muscles.

los.text: Recognise stable and unstable spinal injuries
los.html:
• Three-column model (Denis): anterior (front half of body, anterior longitudinal ligament), middle (back half of body, posterior longitudinal ligament), posterior (arch, facets, posterior ligaments).
StableUnstable
One column only, e.g. wedge compression fracture of the anterior body (osteoporosis), isolated spinous or transverse process fractureTwo or more columns: burst fracture with retropulsion, fracture-dislocation, Chance (flexion-distraction, seatbelt) fracture, Jefferson (C1 burst), dens type II, hangman's (C2 pars)
No risk of further deformity or cord damage under normal loadCan move and damage the cord → immobilise, surgical fixation
  • Initial care: immobilise the spine in trauma; Canadian C-spine rule / NEXUS to decide on imaging; CT is first-line.

los.text: List the anatomical relationships of the spinal cord and spinal nerves, with particular reference to the bones and joints of the vertebral column
los.html:
• Cord ends at L1/L2 in adults (conus medullaris) (L3 at birth)
  • Cauda equina of lumbar and sacral roots continues down
  • Dural sac ends at S2.
Lumbar puncture
  • at L3/4 or L4/5 (Tuffier's line at L4), below the cord.
  • Needle passes skin → supraspinous → interspinous ligament → ligamentum flavum → epidural space → dura and arachnoid → subarachnoid space (CSF).
Spinal nervesC1–7 exit above their vertebra, C8 exits below C7, and from T1 downwards each exits below its vertebra (31 pairs: 8 C, 12 T, 5 L, 5 S, 1 Co).
Intervertebral foramenBounded by pedicles above and below, disc and body in front, facet joint behind → osteophytes and disc bulges compress roots here.
Cord segments don't match vertebraeThe further down, the bigger the mismatch (e.g. the lumbar cord segments sit at T10–L1 vertebrae).
SpacesEpidural (fat, venous plexus: epidural anaesthesia, abscess, haematoma), subdural (potential), subarachnoid (CSF).
Blood supply
  • One anterior spinal artery (front 2/3) and two posterior spinal arteries, reinforced by segmental (radicular) arteries, especially the artery of Adamkiewicz (T9–L2)
  • at risk in aortic surgery.
